sections.h2: Albuquerque at a glance for a seller
sections.html:
New Mexico's biggest city is also the Bernalillo County seat, with 564,559 people in the 2020 census. The Rio Grande runs through a basin that has the Sandia Mountains on its eastern edge and the West Mesa to the west. Houses by the river and houses in the foothills can vary in age, lot type and weather exposure, even in the same ZIP code.

Your bill is tied to the parcel, so the neighborhood name tells you little. Two houses on nearby blocks may belong to different taxing districts.

sections.h2: Who bills property tax in Albuquerque?
sections.html:
Albuquerque addresses get their property tax bill from the Bernalillo County Treasurer, who also collects it, while the county Assessor determines the value. The city itself mails no property tax bill.

Each year the state Department of Finance and Administration sets county rates in September, the Assessor hands the tax roll to the Treasurer by October 1, and bills follow, normally by November 1 or the next business day if that is a weekend.

The Treasurer is at 415 Silver Ave SW downtown, phone (505) 468-7031. Value questions go to the Assessor in the same building, (505) 222-3700.

You pay half by November 10 and half by April 10. Penalties start on December 10 for the first half and on May 10 for the second.

DateWhat happens
January 1Value is fixed for the year and assigned to the owner of record
April 1Last day for the Assessor to mail Notices of Value
30 days after mailingDeadline for protests and exemption applications
October 1Tax roll goes from Assessor to Treasurer
November 1Bills go out by mail and online

April 10Second half due

Confirm any date with the Treasurer before you rely on it, since a deadline that lands on a weekend can shift. Sellers should focus on the November and April payments. Ask the title company how the current half will be split with the buyer, and hold on to your payment confirmations as proof.

sections.h2: What happens if tax goes unpaid
sections.html:
Each month a balance stays unpaid, it gains 1% interest, and a separate 1% penalty accrues too. The penalty stops at 5% and has a $5 floor.

Owners remain liable even if no bill arrives. Many bills come back undelivered after the November mailing, mostly because of outdated mailing addresses, so keep the addresses for your Notice of Value and your bill current. Someone who has left an inherited or rented house is the likeliest to miss a bill.

In June the Treasurer mails delinquent notices. An owner who cannot pay everything at once can call the Treasurer to arrange payments, and a monthly plan is available.

sections.h2: Protesting your value and lowering the bill
sections.html:
You have 30 days from the mailing of the Notice of Value to protest the valuation with the Assessor, and several savings programs use the same 30 days. Protests can be filed through the Assessor's online portal or at the counter, 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal talk with a field appraiser comes first. If the value stays disputed, the Protest Valuation Review Board holds a hearing. After a missed window, the remaining route is to pay first, then ask for a refund through the Second Judicial District Court, 400 Lomas Blvd NW, which charges a $132 filing fee.

Savings programs worth asking about:

  • Head of Family: $2,000 off taxable value, limited to a single property in the state for each household.
  • Veteran exemption: as much as $10,000 off taxable value, backed by a certificate from the state's service commission.
  • Value freeze: open to owners 65 or older earning no more than $42,900 in modified gross income, or disabled owners earning $41,900 or less. It locks the assessed value, though the rate can still change.

There is no homestead exemption in New Mexico. Taxable value is a third of assessed value, and the Head of Family and veteran reductions are taken from that third.

Some Albuquerque subdivisions carry a public improvement district, or PID, which adds a line to the tax bill that pays back bonds for neighborhood infrastructure. The amount per parcel changes from year to year, parcel size and other factors affect it, and a buyer continues the remaining bond payments where the seller left off. An owner may pay a PID off early, and the only exemption on PID payments is the 100% disabled veteran waiver.

Owners inside a district should say so to the buyer and title company at the start. A cash buyer will fold the remaining balance into the offer, and knowing your payoff figure prevents a surprise at the closing table. The county Assessor keeps a page listing the name and boundary of each district.

If the house was ever rented by the night, the city's permit rules apply, and the city does enforce them. Any dwelling, or part of one, let for fewer than 29 consecutive days is a short-term rental.

The permit needs a business license, a floor plan, proof of insurance of at least $250,000 per unit, and a posted Good Neighbor Agreement. The fee is $120 in the first year and $90 for renewals. Operators must also file a monthly lodgers' tax report by the 25th, even when a platform remits the tax. Skipping the permit risks fines and a bar on operating later, so resolve any unpermitted rental history before you put the house on the market.

sections.h2: Notices of Value and the seller's timeline
sections.html:
The Assessor values a property as it stands on January 1 and charges it to whoever is the owner of record that day. Notices of Value go out by April 1, which starts the 30-day period for protests and exemption applications. A spring sale still carries that notice, so tell the buyer and settle in the contract who will file a protest.

When a house passed to an heir without a new deed, mail still goes to the owner of record. Update the record before listing so notices reach someone who can respond.

Paperwork, not buyers, causes most Albuquerque delays. These come up often:

  • A bill mailed to a former address that is now delinquent.
  • A PID balance that was not known until the title search.
  • An unfinished addition that changes the assessed value, or an unpermitted rental.
  • A deed that never moved into an heir's name after a death.

Under any sale route, the title company pays leftover tax out of your proceeds at closing. Look up your balance in the Treasurer's online tax search first. A cash buyer purchasing as is can absorb many of these problems, but will still ask for that number.

faqs.q: Does the City of Albuquerque send its own property tax bill?
faqs.a: No. Bernalillo County bills Albuquerque property owners. The Assessor sets the value, the Treasurer mails the bill and collects, and the state sets the rates each September.

faqs.q: When is Albuquerque property tax due?
faqs.a: Half is due November 10 and half is due April 10. Late fees begin December 10 on the first half and May 10 on the second half.

faqs.q: How much are the late fees on Albuquerque property tax?
faqs.a: Interest is 1% of the unpaid tax each month, and the penalty is 1% each month up to 5%, with a $5 minimum penalty.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Albuquerque house if I still owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid tax, with any penalty and interest, is normally paid from the sale proceeds by the title company at closing. Check the exact balance with the Bernalillo County Treasurer first.

faqs.q: Is there a homestead exemption in Albuquerque?
faqs.a: No. New Mexico has no homestead exemption. The Assessor offers Head of Family, which reduces taxable value by $2,000, plus veteran exemptions and a value freeze for qualifying owners.
